Apple has filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss a lawsuit accusing two former employees, as well as OpenAI and io Products, of stealing its trade secrets. Here's everything you need to know.

Some Background

A few days ago, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss the trade secrets theft lawsuit filed against the company, io Products, Chang Liu, and Tang Tan by Apple.

In the motion, OpenAI claimed that Apple filed its lawsuit "without adequate investigation," and further presented its version of the events that it says led to Apple's lawsuit.

OpenAI's opposition centers on three arguments: that Apple "failed to establish that it possessed trade secrets worthy of protection," that the company "failed to allege acts sufficient to support a claim of trade secret misappropriation," and that it "failed to plausibly allege any injury or ongoing harm."

OpenAI argued, for example, that contrary to Apple's claims, former Apple employee Chang Liu was receiving consultations from a former colleague after his departure, rather than accessing Apple's materials without authorization; while former Apple VP Tang Tan retained Apple's offboarding documents to ensure new hires complied with its security procedures.

OpenAI also argued that Apple's own information management and offboarding practices were partly to blame, claiming that Apple encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts for work, and failed to properly cut off departing employees' access to company materials after they left.

"Apple's lawsuit concerns specific Apple trade secrets, stolen by specific people, in specific ways"

Today, Apple filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss, systematically breaking down OpenAI's arguments and stating that "in short, defendants have not responded at all to the shocking allegations at the core of the complaint."

Apple argued that its original complaint "sufficiently identifies the specific trade secrets misappropriated by defendants," and cited previous cases in which courts found that similarly detailed allegations were sufficient to allow trade secret claims to proceed.

Apple also said that OpenAI's claim that it failed to adequately protect its trade secrets was "equally unavailing," and that OpenAI "dismisses Apple's trade secrets as merely 'supplier relationships,' and then questions whether all 'supplier relationships' are confidential."

Apple further argued that OpenAI was essentially misusing the motion to dismiss mechanism. Here's an excerpt from the relevant documents:

In its opposition, Apple also directly responded to a heavily redacted conversation OpenAI published on its website involving a former colleague still employed at Apple reaching out to Chang Liu to clarify some information about an Apple project.

OpenAI argued that the conversation proved that Apple's characterization of Liu's access to materials after his departure as theft was misleading, because Apple employees themselves had reached out to him for help retrieving materials.
